<cell id="cell-0"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># andesim demo: how many cycles does `hello` take?

`andesim` runs one RISC-V binary on three models with one command:

| Model    | What it is                                      | Speed | Gives you |
|----------|-------------------------------------------------|-------|-----------|
| `fast`   | functional simulation (QEMU)                    | MHz   | program output, instantly |
| `cycle`  | the real Andes core RTL (Verilator)             | kHz   | exact whole-program cycles |
| `hybrid` | `fast` skips ahead, `cycle` measures one region | ~MHz  | exact cycles for the region you mark |

This demo builds one `hello` program and runs it on all three. No engine
knowledge needed: you write C, compile once, and pick a model at run time.</cell id="cell-0">
<cell id="cell-1">import os
from pathlib import Path
root = next(str(d) for d in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents)
            if (d / "build" / "andesim").exists())
os.chdir(root)
os.environ["PATH"] = f"{root}/build:" + os.environ["PATH"]
print("working dir:", root)</cell id="cell-1">

working dir: /home/nick/work/andesim

<cell id="cell-2"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 1. Build `hello`

One compile command. The two flags `-B build/runtime -specs=andesim.specs`
link the portable runtime, so the same ELF runs on every engine.</cell id="cell-2">
<cell id="cell-3">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null      # sets HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"

cat > hello.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
  printf("hello\n");
  return 0;
}
EOF

"$GCC" -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 \
  -B build/runtime -specs=andesim.specs hello.c -o hello.elf

echo "built:"; file hello.elf</cell id="cell-3">

built:


hello.elf: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, UCB RISC-V, RVC, double-float ABI, version 1 (SYSV), staticall

y linked, with debug_info, not stripped

<cell id="cell-4"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 2. Run it fast

`--mode fast` answers "does my program work?" in well under a second.</cell id="cell-4">
<cell id="cell-5">!andesim run --mode fast hello.elf</cell id="cell-5">

hello

<cell id="cell-6"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 3. See which engines are built

`fast` always runs on QEMU, but `cycle` and `hybrid` execute on a specific
RTL core, so you pick one with `--engine`. `andesim list engines` shows
what this repo has built -- the `vsim:*` rows are the cycle-accurate cores
(and `list models` recaps the three models):</cell id="cell-6">
<cell id="cell-7">!andesim list engines</cell id="cell-7">

ENGINE                 TYPE  KIND            XLEN  VLEN  DLEN  ELEN
qemu                   qemu  functional      64    -     -     -   
vsim:ax45mpv_mp2       vsim  cycle-accurate  64    512   512   32  
vsim:ax45mpv_premium   vsim  cycle-accurate  64    512   512   32  
vsim:ax46mpv_advanced  vsim  cycle-accurate  64    512   512   32  

<cell id="cell-8"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 4. Same binary, cycle accurate

`--mode cycle` runs the same ELF on the real Andes core RTL. No rebuild.
The `cycles simulated` line is the exact whole-program cycle count.

We name one of the engines above with `--engine` (here, `vsim:ax45mpv_premium`):</cell id="cell-8">
<cell id="cell-9">!andesim run --mode cycle --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf</cell id="cell-9">

Copyright (C) 2013-2026 Andes Technology Corporation. All rights reserved.
Version : unknown



[[32minfo[m] loading segment: addr=0x100000, memsz=37160, filesz=36320
[[32minfo[m] hart 0 reset vector: 0x100000


hello


[[32minfo[m] sim_control: received command 0x0
[[32minfo[m] sim_control: got exit 0, stopping
[[32minfo[m] Exit PC: 100488
[[32minfo[m] Core 0 last PCs: 0x100488 0x10048a 
[[32minfo[m] 3573 cycles simulated
[[32minfo[m] 0.413s elapsed, 8651.332Hz

<cell id="cell-10"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>`hello` finishes in a fraction of a second here, but RTL simulation runs
at kHz: a real workload takes hours this way. And the count includes
everything: boot, runtime setup, exit. Usually you only care about one
region. That is what `hybrid` is for.

## 5. Mark the region you care about

Wrap the region with two markers from `<andesim/ROI.h>` and recompile.
The markers are RISC-V HINT instructions, i.e. NOPs: they cost nothing,
and the marked binary still runs everywhere, even on real silicon.

Here we measure exactly one `printf`:</cell id="cell-10">
<cell id="cell-11">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"

cat > hello.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>
#include <andesim/ROI.h>

int main(void)
{
  andesim_ROI_begin();   /* start measuring here */
  printf("hello\n");
  andesim_ROI_end();     /* stop measuring here */
  return 0;
}
EOF

"$GCC" -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 \
  -B build/runtime -specs=andesim.specs hello.c -o hello.elf

echo "rebuilt with markers"
</cell id="cell-11">

rebuilt with markers

<cell id="cell-12"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>### Markers are free

The marked binary is still a normal program. On `fast` (or on silicon) the
markers do nothing:</cell id="cell-12">
<cell id="cell-13">!andesim run --mode fast hello.elf</cell id="cell-13">

hello

<cell id="cell-14"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 6. Hybrid: skip ahead fast, measure exactly

`--mode hybrid --trigger marker` runs everything before the first marker
on the fast engine, then hands the live program state to the RTL engine,
which executes the marked region cycle by cycle.</cell id="cell-14">
<cell id="cell-15">!andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf</cell id="cell-15">

[andesim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium vlen=512 trigger=marker fixture=hello
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)


Copyright (C) 2013-2026 Andes Technology Corporation. All rights reserved.
Version : unknown

hello
[marker window_cycles] 2705  (vsim mcycle=519858667184209 - qemu mcycle=519858667181504)
PASS: --mode hybrid --trigger marker (hello)

<cell id="cell-16"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>The answer is the `[marker window_cycles]` line: the exact number of
cycles the marked region (one `printf`) takes on the real core. Program
output still appears, and the run finishes at near-`fast` speed because
only the marked region touches the RTL.

## 7. No markers? The `--pc-start` / `--pc-end` trigger

`--trigger pc` measures between two boundary PCs passed on the command
line as symbol names or `0x` addresses: `--pc-start` (window opens) and `--pc-end`
(window closes). Nothing in the binary needs to cooperate, so this works even on a
prebuilt binary you cannot recompile -- you just need two addresses
from it.

Go back to the plain `hello` from step 1, no markers:</cell id="cell-16">
<cell id="cell-17">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"

cat > hello.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
  printf("hello\n");
  return 0;
}
EOF

"$GCC" -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 \
  -B build/runtime -specs=andesim.specs hello.c -o hello.elf

echo "rebuilt without markers"
</cell id="cell-17">

rebuilt without markers

<cell id="cell-18"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>Find the window addresses with `objdump`. Here we measure all of
`main`: from its entry to `_exit`, where the program stops:</cell id="cell-18">
<cell id="cell-19">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null
"$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump" -d hello.elf | grep -E '<(main|_exit)>:'</cell id="cell-19">

000000000010007c <main>:
000000000010047c <_exit>:

<cell id="cell-20"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>Take the two addresses and pass them as the window boundaries:</cell id="cell-20">
<cell id="cell-21">!andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger pc --pc-start 0x100074 --pc-end 0x100474 --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf</cell id="cell-21">

[andesim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium vlen=512 trigger=pc fixture=hello
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)


andesim run --mode hybrid: plan step 0: expected exit 200, got 0

<cell id="cell-22"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>Same idea, no markers: `[pc window_cycles]` is the exact cycle count
between the two boundary PCs on the real core. It lands close to the
marker figure above; the small extra is `main`'s prologue and the C
runtime's exit path, which the markers excluded.

## Recap

One source, one compile command, three models, two ways to pick a region:

| Goal                              | Command |
|-----------------------------------|---------|
| Does it work? (instant)           | `andesim run --mode fast hello.elf` |
| Whole-program cycles (slow)       | `andesim run --mode cycle --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf` |
| Cycles for the marked region      | `andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf` |
| Same, without touching the source | `andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger pc --pc-start 0x100074 --pc-end 0x100474 --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf` |

To measure your own program: `#include <andesim/ROI.h>`, wrap the region
with `andesim_ROI_begin()` / `andesim_ROI_end()`, rebuild with the same
two flags, run `hybrid`. If you cannot edit the source, find two boundary
addresses with `objdump` and pass them with `--trigger pc`.

More: `docs/andes_sim_tutorial.ipynb` (all trigger modes and engines),
`docs/USER_GUIDE.md` (full reference).</cell id="cell-22">
<cell id="cell-23"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 8. Debug with GDB

Add `--gdb` and the program pauses at startup, waiting for a debugger to
attach — same `hello.elf` from step 1, no rebuild. It works on both standalone
models:

| Model   | `--gdb` opens                              | Connect GDB to    |
|---------|--------------------------------------------|-------------------|
| `fast`  | QEMU's built-in GDB stub                   | port `1234`       |
| `cycle` | vsim's JTAG port + a GDB server (`$ICEMAN`) | the server's port |

### Fast model

`--mode fast --gdb` opens QEMU's GDB stub on port `1234` (override with
`--gdb-port`). Point the toolchain's `riscv64-unknown-elf-gdb` at it, set a
breakpoint, and run. The cell drives the whole session non-interactively —
break at `main`, continue to the breakpoint, check the PC, then continue to the
end, where the program prints `hello`.</cell id="cell-23">
<cell id="cell-24">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null
GDB="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gdb"

# Start the fast model paused at startup; QEMU's GDB stub listens on :1234.
# The program's own output is captured to prog.out.
andesim run --mode fast --gdb hello.elf > prog.out 2>&1 &
SIM=$!

# Wait for the stub port, then attach GDB and drive it non-interactively.
for i in $(seq 1 100); do ss -ltn 2>/dev/null | grep -q ':1234' && break; sleep 0.1; done
echo "=== GDB session ==="
"$GDB" -batch \
    -ex "target remote :1234" \
    -ex "break main" \
    -ex "continue" \
    -ex "info registers pc" \
    -ex "continue" \
    hello.elf

echo "=== program output (from the fast model) ==="
cat prog.out
wait $SIM 2>/dev/null; rm -f prog.out</cell id="cell-24">

<cell id="cell-25"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>### Cycle model

`--mode cycle --gdb` halts the real core, opens vsim's JTAG port (a standard
OpenOCD remote-bitbang port, `9104`), and launches `$ICEMAN` — your JTAG debug
server — once the hart is halted. Connect GDB to the server and you are stepping
the actual RTL.

On a normal Andes setup that is the whole story: `export ICEMAN=/path/to/ICEman`,
then run the **debug session** cell (the second one below). The **first** cell is
demo-only scaffolding — this host's bundled ICEman ships OpenOCD 0.10, which has a
remote-bitbang bug against vsim, so we stand up a throwaway server from a modern
OpenOCD (0.12+) instead. The session then drives the same `hello.elf` — break at
`main`, run (it prints `hello`), and stop at `_exit`.</cell id="cell-25">
<cell id="cell-26">%%bash
# Demo-only -- skip this on a normal setup. vsim needs a JTAG debug server in
# $ICEMAN; you would just `export ICEMAN=/path/to/ICEman`. This host's bundled
# ICEman ships OpenOCD 0.10 (remote_bitbang bug vs vsim), so we stand up a
# throwaway server instead: a modern OpenOCD (0.12+) wired to vsim's port.
cat > /tmp/vsim-oocd.cfg <<'CFG'
adapter driver remote_bitbang
remote_bitbang host localhost
remote_bitbang port 9104
transport select jtag
set _CHIPNAME riscv
jtag newtap $_CHIPNAME cpu -irlen 5
target create $_CHIPNAME.cpu riscv -chain-position $_CHIPNAME.cpu
gdb_port 1111
init
CFG
printf '#!/bin/bash\nexec openocd -f /tmp/vsim-oocd.cfg\n' > /tmp/iceman-vsim.sh
chmod +x /tmp/iceman-vsim.sh</cell id="cell-26">
<cell id="cell-27">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null
GDB="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gdb"
export ICEMAN=/tmp/iceman-vsim.sh   # the throwaway server from the cell above

# This is the whole user-facing command: cycle model, paused at startup. --gdb
# halts the core, opens vsim's JTAG port, and launches $ICEMAN once it is halted.
andesim run --mode cycle --gdb --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf > /tmp/cyc.log 2>&1 &
SIM=$!

# Wait for the gdb server, then drive GDB: break at main, run (hello prints),
# stop at _exit. Same hello.elf from step 1, no rebuild.
for i in $(seq 1 240); do ss -ltn 2>/dev/null | grep -q ':1111' && break; sleep 0.25; done
echo "=== GDB session (cycle model) ==="
"$GDB" -batch \
    -ex "target remote :1111" \
    -ex "break main" -ex "continue" \
    -ex "break _exit" -ex "continue" \
    -ex "info registers pc" \
    hello.elf

echo "=== program output (from the cycle model) ==="
grep -a hello /tmp/cyc.log
pkill -9 -P "$SIM" 2>/dev/null   # stop vsim (halted child of $SIM)
kill -9 "$SIM" 2>/dev/null        # stop the gdb server
true</cell id="cell-27">

<cell id="cell-28"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>#### How it works under the hood

GDB never talks to vsim directly — three processes form a chain:

```
GDB --(gdb-remote :1111)--> $ICEMAN / OpenOCD --(JTAG bitbang :9104)--> vsim (RTL)
```

vsim exposes a JTAG **remote-bitbang** port; OpenOCD drives that link, speaks the
RISC-V Debug Module protocol to halt / step / read the hart, and re-exports an
ordinary **gdb-remote** server (port `1111`) — the port GDB actually attaches to.
That is why you point GDB at the server's port, not at vsim's `9104`.

`andesim` wires the three together:

1. Fork `vsim` in the background with `--jtag-port 9104 -S`.
2. Poll until that port is listening — OpenOCD does **not** retry the bitbang
   connect, so launching it before vsim is ready would just fail.
3. `exec $ICEMAN`, which bridges the JTAG link to the gdb-remote port.

The one piece of real machinery is the `-S` halt. `--jtag-port` *alone* leaves
the hart free-running, and a debugger attaching over the passive bitbang link can
never catch a running RTL hart — its `dmstatus` oscillates `running` /
`unavailable` and never reaches `allhalted`. So `--gdb` always pairs `--jtag-port`
with `-S`, which halts the hart **in-process, before the port opens**, over the
same Debug-Module path the hybrid handoff uses (`dmactive -> haltreq -> poll
allhalted`). The debugger then attaches to an already-stopped core, and its first
`continue` issues `resumereq` to begin execution.

Implementation: `run_cycle_gdb` in `driver/cmd_run.cpp` (the orchestration above)
and `Simulator::halt_for_debug` in `verilator/src/simulator.hpp` (the in-process
halt).</cell id="cell-28">

Same idea, no markers: `[pc window_cycles]` is the exact cycle count
between the two boundary PCs on the real core. It lands close to the
marker figure above; the small extra is `main`'s prologue and the C
runtime's exit path, which the markers excluded.

## Recap

One source, one compile command, three models, two ways to pick a region:

| Goal                              | Command |
|-----------------------------------|---------|
| Does it work? (instant)           | `andesim run --mode fast hello.elf` |
| Whole-program cycles (slow)       | `andesim run --mode cycle --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf` |
| Cycles for the marked region      | `andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf` |
| Same, without touching the source | `andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger pc --pc-start 0x100074 --pc-end 0x100474 --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf` |

To measure your own program: `#include <andesim/ROI.h>`, wrap the region
with `andesim_ROI_begin()` / `andesim_ROI_end()`, rebuild with the same
two flags, run `hybrid`. If you cannot edit the source, find two boundary
addresses with `objdump` and pass them with `--trigger pc`.

More: `docs/andes_sim_tutorial.ipynb` (all trigger modes and engines),
`docs/USER_GUIDE.md` (full reference).

## 8. Debug with GDB

Add `--gdb` and the program pauses at startup, waiting for a debugger to
attach — same `hello.elf` from step 1, no rebuild. It works on both standalone
models:

| Model   | `--gdb` opens                              | Connect GDB to    |
|---------|--------------------------------------------|-------------------|
| `fast`  | QEMU's built-in GDB stub                   | port `1234`       |
| `cycle` | vsim's JTAG port + a GDB server (`$ICEMAN`) | the server's port |

### Fast model

`--mode fast --gdb` opens QEMU's GDB stub on port `1234` (override with
`--gdb-port`). Point the toolchain's `riscv64-unknown-elf-gdb` at it, set a
breakpoint, and run. The cell drives the whole session non-interactively —
break at `main`, continue to the breakpoint, check the PC, then continue to the
end, where the program prints `hello`.

%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null
GDB="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gdb"

# Start the fast model paused at startup; QEMU's GDB stub listens on :1234.
# The program's own output is captured to prog.out.
andesim run --mode fast --gdb hello.elf > prog.out 2>&1 &
SIM=$!

# Wait for the stub port, then attach GDB and drive it non-interactively.
for i in $(seq 1 100); do ss -ltn 2>/dev/null | grep -q ':1234' && break; sleep 0.1; done
echo "=== GDB session ==="
"$GDB" -batch \
    -ex "target remote :1234" \
    -ex "break main" \
    -ex "continue" \
    -ex "info registers pc" \
    -ex "continue" \
    hello.elf

echo "=== program output (from the fast model) ==="
cat prog.out
wait $SIM 2>/dev/null; rm -f prog.out

### Cycle model

`--mode cycle --gdb` halts the real core, opens vsim's JTAG port (a standard
OpenOCD remote-bitbang port, `9104`), and launches `$ICEMAN` — your JTAG debug
server — once the hart is halted. Connect GDB to the server and you are stepping
the actual RTL.

On a normal Andes setup that is the whole story: `export ICEMAN=/path/to/ICEman`,
then run the **debug session** cell (the second one below). The **first** cell is
demo-only scaffolding — this host's bundled ICEman ships OpenOCD 0.10, which has a
remote-bitbang bug against vsim, so we stand up a throwaway server from a modern
OpenOCD (0.12+) instead. The session then drives the same `hello.elf` — break at
`main`, run (it prints `hello`), and stop at `_exit`.

%%bash
# Demo-only -- skip this on a normal setup. vsim needs a JTAG debug server in
# $ICEMAN; you would just `export ICEMAN=/path/to/ICEman`. This host's bundled
# ICEman ships OpenOCD 0.10 (remote_bitbang bug vs vsim), so we stand up a
# throwaway server instead: a modern OpenOCD (0.12+) wired to vsim's port.
cat > /tmp/vsim-oocd.cfg <<'CFG'
adapter driver remote_bitbang
remote_bitbang host localhost
remote_bitbang port 9104
transport select jtag
set _CHIPNAME riscv
jtag newtap $_CHIPNAME cpu -irlen 5
target create $_CHIPNAME.cpu riscv -chain-position $_CHIPNAME.cpu
gdb_port 1111
init
CFG
printf '#!/bin/bash\nexec openocd -f /tmp/vsim-oocd.cfg\n' > /tmp/iceman-vsim.sh
chmod +x /tmp/iceman-vsim.sh

%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null
GDB="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gdb"
export ICEMAN=/tmp/iceman-vsim.sh   # the throwaway server from the cell above

# This is the whole user-facing command: cycle model, paused at startup. --gdb
# halts the core, opens vsim's JTAG port, and launches $ICEMAN once it is halted.
andesim run --mode cycle --gdb --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf > /tmp/cyc.log 2>&1 &
SIM=$!

# Wait for the gdb server, then drive GDB: break at main, run (hello prints),
# stop at _exit. Same hello.elf from step 1, no rebuild.
for i in $(seq 1 240); do ss -ltn 2>/dev/null | grep -q ':1111' && break; sleep 0.25; done
echo "=== GDB session (cycle model) ==="
"$GDB" -batch \
    -ex "target remote :1111" \
    -ex "break main" -ex "continue" \
    -ex "break _exit" -ex "continue" \
    -ex "info registers pc" \
    hello.elf

echo "=== program output (from the cycle model) ==="
grep -a hello /tmp/cyc.log
pkill -9 -P "$SIM" 2>/dev/null   # stop vsim (halted child of $SIM)
kill -9 "$SIM" 2>/dev/null        # stop the gdb server
true

cells.source:
#### How it works under the hood

GDB never talks to vsim directly — three processes form a chain:

```
GDB --(gdb-remote :1111)--> $ICEMAN / OpenOCD --(JTAG bitbang :9104)--> vsim (RTL)
```

vsim exposes a JTAG **remote-bitbang** port; OpenOCD drives that link, speaks the
RISC-V Debug Module protocol to halt / step / read the hart, and re-exports an
ordinary **gdb-remote** server (port `1111`) — the port GDB actually attaches to.
That is why you point GDB at the server's port, not at vsim's `9104`.

`andesim` wires the three together:

1. Fork `vsim` in the background with `--jtag-port 9104 -S`.
2. Poll until that port is listening — OpenOCD does **not** retry the bitbang
   connect, so launching it before vsim is ready would just fail.
3. `exec $ICEMAN`, which bridges the JTAG link to the gdb-remote port.

The one piece of real machinery is the `-S` halt. `--jtag-port` *alone* leaves
the hart free-running, and a debugger attaching over the passive bitbang link can
never catch a running RTL hart — its `dmstatus` oscillates `running` /
`unavailable` and never reaches `allhalted`. So `--gdb` always pairs `--jtag-port`
with `-S`, which halts the hart **in-process, before the port opens**, over the
same Debug-Module path the hybrid handoff uses (`dmactive -> haltreq -> poll
allhalted`). The debugger then attaches to an already-stopped core, and its first
`continue` issues `resumereq` to begin execution.

Implementation: `run_cycle_gdb` in `driver/cmd_run.cpp` (the orchestration above)
and `Simulator::halt_for_debug` in `verilator/src/simulator.hpp` (the in-process
halt).
